ceviri.33: How long does keyword research take?
ceviri.34: The scope sets the time. On a local business offering a single service, a few days is enough. On a catalogue with hundreds of products, building the pool and tagging it can stretch to two weeks. The list grows over time, but the initial setup is done once.
ceviri.35: How many keywords should a small business start with?
ceviri.36: A core list of thirty to forty terms is enough for most SMEs. Start with the service that brings in revenue.
ceviri.38: On the contrary — a query with a sharp purpose carries high value even at low volume. A term a hundred people search while ready to buy can bring more business than one ten thousand people search out of curiosity. Always read the volume together with the purpose.
ceviri.39: Can I understand search intent without a measurement dashboard?
ceviri.40: Largely, yes. Type the query and look at the type of the first ten results: are guide articles, category pages or product pages in the majority? The dominant type shows the kind of content that query expects. That observation gives you a useful direction without needing an expensive setup.
ceviri.41: Should I open two separate pages for the same keyword?
ceviri.42: Usually no. Two pages carrying the same purpose split each other's ranking. Gather the queries onto one strong page; open a second page only if the purpose really is different.
ceviri.43: Does competitors' keyword list guide us?
ceviri.44: A competitor's list is a starting point, not a target. The queries your competitor ranks for show the language of the market. Even so, their resources and brand strength differ from yours. Rather than copying, look for the long-tail areas your competitors have left empty.
ceviri.45: Which details should we watch in Turkish searches?
ceviri.46: Four details make a difference in Turkish queries. The first is suffixed forms: users often type “çelik kapı fiyatları” (steel door prices, plural) rather than “çelik kapı fiyatı” (singular). The second is writing without diacritics; there is a large audience searching “isitici” instead of “ısıtıcı” (heater). The third is regional differences in usage, that is, the same product having different names from city to city. The fourth is settled use of English equivalents; in some sectors users never search the Turkish term at all. Bring all four into the pool as you build the list. Those four details are what bring your list closer to the real language of search.
ceviri.47: How often should we review the keyword list?
ceviri.48: A review once a quarter is enough for most sectors. When there's a new product, a new region or a sudden shift in the sector's agenda, refresh the list without waiting.

ceviri.62: Why Is Keyword Research the Compass for Your Content?
ceviri.63: Why does a site's traffic stand still? The answer usually lies not in the technical foundations but in the keywords you're targeting. Many SMEs in Türkiye produce content in their own internal language, while the customer types something completely different into the search box. The method that closes the distance between those two languages is called keyword research. In this piece we open the mechanism up: how we measure demand, and how we read intent.
ceviri.64: The right keyword is the compass that sets the direction of the content.
ceviri.66: What Does Measuring Search Demand Mean?
ceviri.67: Keyword research is the work that measures which phrases a subject is asked about in search engines, and how often. The measurement reads the monthly search count, the intensity of competition and the purpose behind the query together. Volume on its own misleads. When those figures come side by side, a clear direction emerges. Measurement is the first step of producing content.
ceviri.68: Search demand is a measurable signal showing how many people ask about a subject and with which words. A site that doesn't read the signal writes answers to questions nobody is asking. You say “dermocosmetic set”; the customer types “skincare set”. Your lost visitor stands in exactly that gap. Keyword research measures the gap and closes it.
ceviri.69: Competition hardens every year too. According to the Ministry of Trade's
ceviri.71: — ETBİS is Türkiye's e-commerce information system — the number of businesses trading online reached 634,611. A business that leaves its keyword choices to chance stays invisible in that crowd.
ceviri.73: we start every project with measurement.
ceviri.74: Winning the Demand Behind the Word
ceviri.75: When a page ranks, you don't win a keyword; you win the attention of the person who typed it. The difference between the query “air conditioner” and “quiet air conditioner recommendation for an office” is the distance left to a purchase. The first query carries curiosity, the second carries a decision.
ceviri.76: The Triangle of Volume, Difficulty and Intent
ceviri.77: The monthly search count shows the size of the demand, the difficulty level the hardness of the competition, and the intent the purpose of the query. If one of those figures is missing, the decision is crippled. A high-volume term whose purpose doesn't fit brings traffic to the site, not enquiries. So what does a term with a sharp purpose and low volume do? It brings few visitors; a significant share of them walk all the way to the enquiry form.
ceviri.78: How Do We Read Search Intent?
ceviri.79: We read intent by looking at the common form of the pages ranking for a query. Search intent is the concept that defines the type of result a user wants to reach when they type a query. The kind of content Google lists on the first page reveals what that query expects. The method rests on observation; guesswork doesn't come into it. You can reach the same conclusion by reading the screen rather than a dashboard.
ceviri.80: Intent analysis is the stage that makes a keyword list useful. Two terms with the same volume go to different pages because they carry different purposes. Teams that skip this stage don't get conversions. Keyword research carried out without the intent layer is left half done.
ceviri.81: Internet access in Türkiye has spread across a broad base;
ceviri.83: — TurkStat is Türkiye's statistical institute — measure that spread regularly. As the user profile widens, the phrases describing the same service diversify. Short and question-form queries ask for their own layer in your list.
ceviri.85: Informational intent wants to learn, navigational intent goes to a particular brand, commercial intent compares options, and transactional intent is ready to buy. Each class wants a different type of page. A guide article corresponds to informational intent, a category page to commercial intent, and a product page to transactional intent.
ceviri.86: The Results Page Is the Most Reliable Evidence
ceviri.87: The quickest way to understand a query's purpose is to read the results page. If eight of the first ten results are list articles, that query wants a guide. A screen full of category pages, meanwhile, gives away a user looking for a product. The screen itself is the evidence; no assumption is needed.
ceviri.88: The Early Sign of an Intent Mismatch
ceviri.89: If your page ranks, clicks come in, and the session length is measured in seconds, there's a mismatch. The user hasn't found what they were after. You see the same signal when a visitor returns to the results page for a second search. In that case change the type of the page; the keyword can stay where it is.
ceviri.90: The Keyword Selection Mechanism: From Pool to Priority
ceviri.91: Keyword research reduces a broad pool of candidates to a short list ordered by business value. We widen the pool, tag it by intent, sift out the irrelevant terms and prioritise what remains. A written criterion governs the process from start to finish. The output of each step is the input of the next. A shorter list gathers up the resources that were scattering.
ceviri.92: The selection starts with a wide pool and ends with a narrow list. The road between them has five steps. The sift is the heart of keyword research.
ceviri.94: your service names, your product categories and the questions coming from your customers build the first pool.
ceviri.96: for every seed term, add the synonyms, the local usages and the question forms.
ceviri.98: give every query an informational, navigational, commercial or transactional tag.
ceviri.100: take out the terms that don't match your service area and the ones with weak relevance.
ceviri.102: order the remaining terms by business value and by a level of competition you can reach.
ceviri.103: We apply this mechanism in the first phase of
ceviri.105: . On the store side, category and filter pages go through the same sift; on the
ceviri.107: side the list is shaped by the category tree. Your content calendar is born from that file.
ceviri.109: The wider the keyword pool is at the start of the research, the more accurate the sift. For a manufacturer, “office chair” comes from a seed; “office chair with lumbar support” comes from real demand. At the widening stage our aim is variety; a long but single-coloured list is no use at the sifting table.
ceviri.111: For a term to stay on the list it has to be relevant to your service, sit at a level of competition you can reach, and find a real page to correspond to. A term with nothing to correspond to gives birth to an empty page. Sifting shortens the list; the real gain is your resources flowing in one direction without scattering.
ceviri.112: Why Do Long-Tail Keywords Benefit SMEs?
ceviri.113: Because the competition is sparse, small sites rank far faster on long-tail queries. Long-tail keywords are queries of three or more words, low in search count but clear in purpose. As the tail lengthens, the variety of queries grows; the same demand spreads across more phrases. That spread opens a door for a small site.
ceviri.114: On general terms, the first page is full of large brands that have been investing for years. Competing there is a test of patience for an SME. The long tail, meanwhile, is an area that hasn't yet grown crowded. “Crane” takes you to the crowd; “electric warehouse crane hire” takes you to the right customer. The long tail is the most productive layer in keyword research.
ceviri.115: You can follow the size of the market through public data;
ceviri.116: the Ministry of Trade's e-commerce outlook announcement
ceviri.117: shares the number of businesses. In a market growing more crowded, keyword research is the cheapest way to stand apart.
ceviri.118: Competition Thins Out, Conversion Goes Up
ceviri.119: As the query lengthens, the picture in the user's head sharpens. Someone typing a five-word query knows what they want and is one step closer to the enquiry form. So what does a visitor arriving from a general term do? Most of the time they browse and close the page.
ceviri.121: We call gathering queries that share the same purpose onto a single page clustering. Instead of twenty weak pages for twenty separate queries, you build three strong ones. Clustering logic both prevents a patchwork pile of content and tightens the links between pages. That's how topic authority accumulates, page by page.

ceviri.124: Hand Your Keyword Research to a Professional
ceviri.125: Handing the research over doesn't mean giving up control; it means transferring the measurement load to a specialist team. Keyword research is a specialism that brings reading data and sector knowledge to the same table. Your team knows its own business, and we know how to read search data. When the two meet, the list becomes both realistic and workable.
ceviri.126: At most SMEs, marketing sits on one person's shoulders; there's no time left to tag hundreds of queries. We turn that job into a structure: we build the pool, tag it, and hand over the priority list in a single file.
ceviri.127: The output of the research is a keyword map, not an ornamental table. If you'd like to compare your own list with ours, get in touch through
ceviri.129: . We make the first assessment, you make the decision.
ceviri.130: What Changes When You Work with Us?
ceviri.131: The first thing that changes after keyword research is clarity. You see which page was written for which query, and why each term was sifted out, with the reasoning. Speed rises too; your team comes out of the argument about words and goes back to producing. Because the list rests on a shared criterion, consistency follows by itself.
